Article Title: Indian consulate in UAE issues warning over biometric fraud targeting nationals
Article Text:
The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.

NEW DELHI: The consulate general of India in Dubai has warned Indian nationals in the UAE, particularly blue-collar workers, against handing over biometric data. The warning advised the workers against unauthorised agents claiming to help with visa regularisation, Emergency Certificates, Exit Permits, Emirates IDs or employment, after reports of fraud involving the misuse of fingerprints and facial scans.In an advisory issued on Monday, the consulate said it had received information about individuals and agents allegedly exploiting Indians seeking assistance with immigration and documentation procedures. The fraudsters reportedly ask victims to provide fingerprints or face scans, which can then be used without their knowledge to conduct financial transactions, open bank accounts or obtain loans and credit cards in their names.The consulate cautioned that such misuse could leave victims liable for financial obligations or transactions they did not authorise. In some cases, those affected could also face multiple fines, travel bans and even imprisonment.The advisory urged nationals not to share their passports, Emirates IDs, biometric data, including eye, face or fingerprint scans, or personal and financial credentials with unauthorised individuals or agencies under any circumstances.It also clarified that biometric information required for procedures such as exit permits, Emirates IDs or visa regularisation must be provided only at official UAE Government facilities or counters. People were specifically warned against submitting such information through private individuals, agents or third-party service providers claiming to be authorised by UAE authorities.The consulate also sought to dispel a potential source of confusion by stating that biometric information is not required for certain consular services.The advisory said the Consulate General of India in Dubai and the Embassy of India in Abu Dhabi "DO NOT require any fingerprint scan or face/eye scan from applicants for the issuance of a passport or emergency certificate."It warned that any person or agent demanding such information while claiming to represent the Indian Embassy or consulate would be engaging in fraudulent activity and should not be entertained.Indians approached by unauthorised individuals seeking biometric data or Emirates IDs have been advised to contact the Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra through the toll-free number 80046342, WhatsApp or SMS at 00971543090571, or email pbsk.dubai@mea.gov.in to verify credentials or seek assistance.The consulate urged Indian nationals living in or visiting the UAE to exercise caution, independently verify the credentials of anyone offering immigration or documentation-related services, and report suspicious activity to the Indian consulate and the relevant UAE authorities.
Article Summary: The warning advised the workers against unauthorised agents claiming to help with visa regularisation, Emergency Certificates, Exit Permits, Emirates IDs or employment. The fraudsters reportedly ask victims to provide fingerprints or face scans, which can then be used without their knowledge to conduct financial transactions.

Article Title: Flyers asked to give handwriting samples after threat note causes Air India Express international flight to divert
Article Text:
Representative image (PTI photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Indian security establishment have finally decided to take the menace of hoax bomb threats that cause expensive diversions head on. An Air India Express Dammam-Delhi nonstop was forced to divert to Ahmedabad after a tissue paper with the words “bomb red 430” written on it and a box, both in black ink, drawn on it was found in the lav. After landing in Ahmedabad and following the required protocol, the security authorities additionally decided to conduct a handwriting test on all the 32 passengers and see if the expensive prank was played by one of them.“They asked the airline to give the same tissue paper and then organised the same colour pen. Six tissues were sought for each passenger. Now let us see if they find a match,” said sources. It is not yet known if this test managed to nab the person who allegedly wrote this threat note.The standard protocol for such situations is taking the aircraft to a remote parking bay; checking all passengers and cabin and check-in baggage thoroughly before clearing it to take off again. All this was followed on Monday too at Ahmedabad. The handwriting test was conducted on top of that.An Air India Express spokesperson said: “One of our flights from Dammam to Delhi was diverted to Ahmedabad as a precaution and in keeping with security protocols after being notified of a specific bomb threat.The government-appointed bomb threat assessment committee (BTAC) was alerted immediately, and all security procedures promptly initiated. The flight landed and all guests have been disembarked safely. The aircraft will be released for operations after necessary security checks are completed.”Indian carriers have suffered huge losses due to hoax threats in recent years. While tracking a call making such a claim is difficult due to advancement in technology, tackling on board threatening notes if written by someone onboard the affected flight could help tackle this menace. Monday’s handwriting test decision, say sources, was taken by BCAS and CISF. “Why the same has not been done in the past beats us,” said a senior pilot.Airlines and airports in India had received 999 hoax bomb threats between Jan 1 and Nov 14, 2024 — more than 10 times the number in 2023. The threats to both domestic and international flights were made mostly through social media and had disrupted air travel in India.
Article Summary: Airlines and airports in India had received 999 hoax bomb threats between Jan 1 and Nov 14, 2024 — more than 10 times the number in 2023. The threats to both domestic and international flights were made mostly through social media and had disrupted air travel in India.

Article Title: 'No double standards on terrorism': PM Modi's message at SCO summit in presence of Pak PM Shehbaz Sharif
Article Text:
PM Modi called for dismantling the entire ecosystem that enables terrorism at SCO

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday said there can be no “double standards” in the fight against terrorism and called for dismantling its entire ecosystem, including financing, recruitment, radicalisation and safe havens.Addressing the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, PM Modi described terrorism as a “grave challenge to all of humanity” and said the fight against it cannot be limited to a mindset of “action-reaction”.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalization, and safe havens. We must speak in one voice that there can be no place for double standards on this serious issue,” he said.“Those countries that use terrorism as an instrument of their policy, and provide shelter and support to terrorists, must be sent a strong message that terrorism cannot be a ‘strategic asset’ for anyone,” the Prime Minister added.He also outlined "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity" as the three pillars of India’s vision for the SCO, with peace and security forming the first pillar.“Our shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan,” he said, adding that India would continue its development and humanitarian assistance to the Afghan people.On the West Asia crisis, Modi said conflicts in one region can have repercussions across the world, affecting “energy security, maritime trade, and supply chains of the entire world”.“The countries of the Global South have to bear the maximum brunt of this. Therefore, India's call has been that the solution to all tensions and wars is not possible on the battlefield, but only through Dialogue and Diplomacy,” he said.The Prime Minister also flagged drug trafficking as a serious threat to the younger generation and regional security, calling for stronger cooperation through SCO mechanisms dealing with security threats, organised crime, information security and narcotics. “We must make them effective mediums for practical coordination and timely action,” PM Modi said.He further stressed that SCO cooperation should translate into tangible benefits for people, with people-to-people ties placed at the centre of the grouping’s future agenda.“The true measure of our success should be how many new opportunities our efforts have created for young people, how many new markets have opened up for our entrepreneurs, how much our farmers have benefited from technology, and how much better the lives of our citizens have become,” he said.Kyrgyzstan President Sadyr Japarov is hosting the summit and serving as its chairman. PM Modi is attending alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders of SCO member states.
Article Summary: PM Modi called for dismantling the entire ecosystem that enables terrorism at SCO Summit. He outlined "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity" as the three pillars of India’s vision for the SCO. He also flagged drug trafficking as a serious threat to the younger generation and regional security.

Article Title: SC asks Centre, states why retail acid sale cannot be completely banned to curb attacks
Article Text:
The SC bench asked the Centre and states to respond within four weeks on a policy decision to either ban the retail sale of acid or impose strict restrictions on it. (Photo: PTI)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday asked the Centre and the states why retail sale of acid should not be banned after an acid attack survivor complained that the SC-prompted 2013 guidelines of the Union government remain on paper even as girls continue to suffer physical disfigurement and lifelong mental trauma from acid attacks.Continuing with its strong stance against those jilted lovers accused of throwing acid on girls leading to severe physical disfigurement, loss of eyesight and lifelong mental trauma, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the Centre and states to respond within four weeks on a policy decision to either ban retail sale of acid or impose strict restrictions on it.This direction came after acid attack survivor Shaheen Malik, who runs an NGO to help girls who suffered trauma and scars of acid attacks, told the bench that every day three girls face a similar fate and there should be a complete ban on the retail sale of acid. She cited a case of three girls, two from Okhla in Delhi and one in Haryana, who were blinded by acid attacks. “How many more girls must suffer,” she asked while pushing for a complete ban.Accepting that acid should be supplied for the purpose of research and educational institutions, the bench said banning across-the-counter sale is the first option. In the alternative, it proposed whether retail sale of acid can be restricted only to those who are above 50 years of age after they give in writing the purpose behind such purchases.The data should be collated on a dashboard for ready reference of law-enforcing agencies on acid available in private hands.Senior advocate Saurabh Kirpal told the bench that strict guidelines framed by the SC in the Laxmi case in 2013 said acid continues to be available across the counter. The bench said the 2013 guidelines must have become obsolete now and asked additional solicitor general Archana Pathak Dave to submit fresh guidelines from the Centre on this issue.The bench also sought a status report on implementation of its May 9 directions to the states and Centre seeking schemes for rehabilitation of acid attack survivors, which could include preferential government employment and, in the absence of which, a monthly honorarium, lifelong free medical treatment and free education. SC also said it is desirable to include in the school curriculum the preventive measures, post-attack treatment and emergency protocol.
Article Summary: The Supreme Court asked the Centre and states to respond within four weeks on a policy decision to either ban retail sale of acid or impose strict restrictions on it. The direction came after acid attack survivor Shaheen Malik, who runs an NGO to help girls who suffered trauma and scars of acid attacks, told the bench that every day three girls face a similar fate.

Article Title: Kenney, Sikh leader share dais as Bhagwat makes global Hindu call
Article Text:
Bhagwat’s visit came despite demands from New Democratic Party and civil-society groups that he be denied entry to Canada. The venue was disclosed shortly before the programme amid security concerns.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A day after telling a New York audience that a Hindu who wanted Muslims excluded from India could not remain a Hindu, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat Monday used his first visit to Canada to cast Hindus as builders of an “exemplary society” worldwide and India as a “vishwaguru” serving humanity, not a “mahashakti” seeking dominance.The speeches shared themes of oneness, but differed in emphasis. In New York, amid protests and criticism of RSS, Bhagwat addressed concerns about exclusion; in Toronto, he explained how Hindu society should organise and lead internationally without imposing its beliefs.“The word Hindu cannot be defined by any specific language, through any specific worship or through any living style,” he said. The dais reflected that wider outreach: former Alberta premier and federal cabinet minister Jason Kenney and Kashmir Singh Dhaliwal of the Khalsa Diwan Society joined Bhagwat, placing a senior Canadian political figure and a representative of a Sikh institution alongside the RSS chief at a gathering opposed by sections of the South Asian community.“We have to build our society in every country, all over the world, which is an exemplary society for the world,” Bhagwat said at the “Hindu Vishwa Bandhu — Embrace the World in Friendship” event. The programme in Vaughan, in the Greater Toronto Area, was organised by Canadian Hindus for Outreach, Relations and Dialogue.Presenting India’s global role as one based on service rather than power, Bhagwat said: “It became ‘vishwaguru’, not ‘mahashakti’.”Whenever help had been sought during an international crisis, he said, India had not refused. “This is the tradition. This is the DNA of Bharat.”Bhagwat said the RSS organised Hindus “exactly for this purpose — and nothing else”, describing the purpose as developing individuals who would dedicate themselves to serving humanity.The RSS chief coupled the call for organisation with a message on civic responsibility. People connected with India but settled elsewhere, he said, “have to be honest, contributing citizens of that country”. At the same time, they should take to the world an outlook in which individuals, society and the environment could progress without harming one another.He said this should be done through conduct rather than imposition. “We don’t force,” Bhagwat said. “We are the leaders who lead from within and lead by example.” He added: “Hindus respect all. Hindus accept all.”Going beyond the familiar expression “unity in diversity”, Bhagwat said Hindu tradition also recognised “diversities of unity”. Different identities, he argued, were expressions of an underlying oneness. “Diversity is never a problem for unity,” he said. “All the diversities are expressions of unity.”Bhagwat’s visit came despite demands from New Democratic Party and civil-society groups that he be denied entry to Canada. The venue was disclosed shortly before the programme amid security concerns.
Article Summary: Bhagwat’s visit came despite demands from New Democratic Party and civil-society groups that he be denied entry to Canada. The venue was disclosed shortly before the programme amid security concerns. Bhagwat said the RSS organised Hindus “exactly for this purpose — and nothing else”

Article Title: CM Vijay releases Mettur Dam water for delta irrigation
Article Text:
(Photo: AM Shudhagar) The Mettur dam is traditionally opened on June 12 every year to facilitate the cultivation of kuruvai in the Cauvery Delta region. The opening was delayed this year as water levels in the Cauvery basin reservoir remained low.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

METTUR (SALEM): Chief minister of Tamil Nadu C Joseph Vijay on Tuesday released water from the Mettur Dam to meet the drinking water requirements and support samba cultivation in the Cauvery delta districts, the rice granaries of the state.As of Tuesday morning, the dam’s water level stood at 91.56 feet, with a storage of 54.452 tmc ft and an inflow of 10,857 cusecs. Water Resources Department officials said the release will be continuously monitored and regulated according to irrigation needs.Departments including Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Water Resources, and Revenue and Disaster Management have been directed to coordinate with district administrations to ensure effective utilisation. The government stressed that every cubic foot of water must benefit farmers, warning against illegal pumping, unauthorised extraction, and violations of permitted irrigation schemes.Joint monitoring teams comprising officials from the Electricity Distribution Corporation, Water Resources Department, Revenue Department, and Police will patrol day and night to prevent misuse.Reaffirming Tamil Nadu’s legal entitlement to Cauvery water, the chief minister said the state would not compromise on its rights upheld by the Cauvery Arbitration Final Award and the Supreme Court’s 2018 verdict.The government continues to pursue legal and administrative measures to secure the state’s share.Acknowledging the deficit in the southwest monsoon and the impact of El Niño, Vijay said the release was a planned measure to manage limited resources and safeguard samba cultivation. Farmers were urged to adopt medium-duration rice varieties and water-saving methods such as direct seeding.“Let us use water sparingly, ensure it reaches the end user, and make samba cultivation a success,” the chief minister appealed.
Article Summary: The Mettur dam is traditionally opened on June 12 every year to facilitate the cultivation of kuruvai. The opening was delayed this year as water levels in the Cauvery basin reservoir remained low. As of Tuesday morning, the dam’s water level stood at 91.56 feet.

Article Title: 'Chhatron ki Goonj' reaches Indore as Rahul eyes BJP's vulnerabilities with "best city" as example
Article Text:
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi. (Photo: ANI)

NEW DELHI: Amid continuing reverberations from Rahul Gandhi ’s girl-students rally in Pune, the Congress youth outreach “Chhatron ki Goonj” is set to move to another BJP stronghold, the education hub of Madhya Pradesh.Sources said the next episode of “chhatron ki goonj” will be held in Indore on Sep 12.In what is a carefully crafted strategy to challenge the ruling party with the “angry demographic” that led the Jantar Mantar protest, Congress has picked the venue owing to the fact that there has been a history of paper leaks in the state including the infamous examination scandal “Vyapam scam”. Besides, the opposition has won two by-elections “against the might of the state”, the latest being Datia assembly last month.Sources said the party considered a few cities, including in the Congress-ruled states in the south, but then decided on Indore in a bid to continue pressuring the BJP.While the city is a students’ hub and also has a fair share of urban and middle-class population, it has been in the negative spotlight for repeated infrastructural crises – the most sensational being 24 deaths from consuming sewage contaminated water in February 2026.A smart city road, said to be constructed at the cost of Rs 40 crore, collapsed recently, hogging the headlines. Also, there have been allegations of corruption targeting the CM.The “chhatron ki goonj” started in Kota in Rajasthan (June) and then moved to Dehradun (July) and then Prayagraj (August), focusing on examination and employment issues. But in Pune last month, Rahul changed tack when he made it an exclusive event for girls, and his interactive speech around gender justice and “manusmriti” received favourable feedback besides triggering the opponent BJP.The “CKG” strategists are chuffed by the reaction and said the programme will move across the nation with the objective of becoming a “brand” that the youth will associate with.After Indore, the party may choose a city in any of the Congress-ruled states in the south to cover a key region with a strong youth population.Recently, the Congress Working Committee decided that “CKG” will be held in 800 cities and towns – which means one in every district. Sources said Rahul may personally attend around 20 of them, while the rest will become a vehicle for the party to woo the youth.
Article Summary: The next episode of “chhatron ki goonj’ will be held in Indore on Sep 12. Congress has picked the venue owing to the fact that there has been a history of paper leaks in the state including the infamous examination scandal “Vyapam scam”

UTTARAKHAND: Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami has intervened to secure urgent medical aid for an eight-year-old boy suffering from a lifelong debilitating health condition.This comes after the Chief Minister visited a local food stall in Lohiahead, where the boy's father shared their struggle.Following CM Dhami's directions, Udham Singh Nagar District Magistrate Nitin Singh Bhadauria, along with Chief Medical Officer Dr SK Goswami, a team of doctors, Chief Development Officer Divesh Shasani and Sub-Divisional Magistrate Tushar Saini, visited Ravi Sharma's residence, whose eight-year-old son has been suffering from a health condition since childhood and is unable to move his hands and leg, according to a release from the CMO.CM Dhami visited Ravi Sharma's shop in Lohiahead on Sunday to have tikki. During the interaction, Ravi Sharma told the Chief Minister about his son Dev and his condition. The child has been undergoing treatment since birth, including treatment at Indresh Hospital in Dehradun.Orthopaedic specialist Dr HS Airi and the Chief Medical Officer examined the child and reviewed his previous medical history and treatment records.After the examination and assessment of his past treatment history, the doctors suggested that an MRI scan be conducted first, following which further treatment would be decided. The District Magistrate immediately directed officials to arrange the child's MRI scan the very next day.He said that the administration would provide a vehicle and necessary assistance to take the child and his parents to the district hospital. He assured the family that every possible effort would be made to ensure the child receives proper treatment and that no stone would be left unturned in his care.Earlier, on August 28, Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami also announced the development of modern, high-tech toilets across the state, keeping in mind the convenience, safety and dignity of women."These facilities will be equipped with modern amenities and will give special attention to cleanliness, privacy, security and the essential needs of women."The Chief Minister said that the dignity and respect of women are among the state government's highest priorities.
Article Summary: Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami has intervened to secure urgent medical aid for an eight-year-old boy suffering from a lifelong debilitating health condition. Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday was seen sharing warm handshakes and a brief exchange with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek.The interaction took place as the leaders gathered at the Yrys Ordo Congress Hall for the official group photograph, a traditional feature of the annual SCO summit. PM Modi was seen greeting Xi and Putin as the leaders assembled for the photograph.The three leaders are among the heads of state and government attending the summit, hosted by Kyrgyzstan President Sadyr Japarov, who is also chairing the gathering.A roundtable discussion involving the SCO member states was also held at the venue. Alongside PM Modi, Xi and Putin, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Kazakhstan President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Tajik President Emomali Rahmon are attending the summit.The 26th SCO Leadership Summit brings together the organisation's 10 member states, along with 15 partner countries and two observer countries.The grouping represents around 25% of global GDP and focuses on cooperation in areas including security, connectivity, economic development and regional stability.PM Modi, who will address the summit, is expected to outline India's priorities of security, connectivity and opportunity. India has been a full member of the SCO since 2017.The summit is also being held in the expanded "SCO Plus" format, bringing together leaders from a wider group of countries. Those attending include Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith and Togolese President Faure Gnassingbe.

Article Title: Translating the Reliance ethos into a blueprint for nation-building
Article Text:
Translating familial empathy into enterprise resilience

Democratising technology for a billion aspirations

Reclaiming soft power and passing the baton

There is a prevailing wisdom in global business schools that suggests the larger an enterprise grows, the colder it must become. Scale, the theory goes, demands a clinical detachment. Yet, in the heart of India's corporate landscape, a remarkably different experiment has been playing out for decades. Here, the traditional Indian family ethos has not been discarded as an archaic social structure but rather leveraged as a sophisticated business strategy.The recently released Reliance documentary, 'Parvah Hai Toh Parivar Hai', pulls back the curtain on this machinery. It offers a case study of what happens when the ethics of a household extend to a conglomerate employing hundreds of thousands, and ultimately to a nation of 1.4 billion people.Stripping away the complex financial jargon often associated with India's largest enterprise, the film reveals a foundational philosophy rooted in care, trust, and self-reliance. It asks a compelling question: can familial empathy actually drive a nation's socio-economic trajectory?At the corporate level, this paternalistic model is far more than a warm metaphor. It operates as a highly effective structural framework. The fundamental premise that care defines a family dictates how the company handles its human capital. During moments of intense crisis, such as health emergencies or natural disasters, this responsibility translates into the swift mobilisation of healthcare, isolation facilities, and emergency resources.This culture of protective support builds a rare institutional resilience, fostering a fiercely loyal ecosystem. Recalling the early days of setting up Jio Studios, an executive describes the deep personal involvement of the leadership. "I remember Mukesh Bhai and Manoj Bhai laying out their vision for the media business," she notes. "I remember thinking, do I have to pay to work here because this kind of mentorship is something that money cannot buy. "When creative and professional ventures face unexpected headwinds, this cushion of corporate confidence remains largely intact. Actor Ranveer Singh, reflecting on his collaborations with the conglomerate, highlighted this unusual patience. "I was given all the love, all the support and all the encouragement even at a time when my movies were not doing well," he shares in the film. "Career ups and downs. But to have received that kind of support meant a lot to me. It's nothing short of a blessing, an honour and a privilege to be associated with the Ambani family."However, the true test of any family-led business model lies in its ability to step outside its own perimeter and serve the wider community. For Reliance, modern nation building has meant translating massive corporate capacity into accessible public utility. Having already rewired India's digital landscape by making high-speed data universal through Jio, the enterprise is now looking towards the next frontier.The leadership frequently questions how their scale affects the masses. According to the documentary, the next step involves using new age technologies to bridge socio-economic gaps. "How does it affect the 1.4 billion people of India as we democratise information," the film asks, noting that generative artificial intelligence is "now democratising intelligence amongst 1.4 billion people."The ambition is to create tools that serve every stratum of society. The narrative paints a stark rural reality, envisioning a person in Bhagalpur "able to really use an AI tutor to teach himself or a farmer who is able to really understand what his food productivity would be." As the leadership points out, with this knowledge, "he is able to think more, he is able to do more, he is able to earn more and that is I think the ultimate goal for us. "Recognising that there are many Indias cutting across different income classes, the company is pivoting toward voice-first interfaces designed for the country's vast linguistic diversity. The documentary rightly points out that "Indians actually converse with technology by voice first rather than text." It is framed as a massive opportunity "which truly only an Indian company can solve." This ethos of mass accessibility comes directly from the top. As Mukesh Ambani directed his team regarding their massive streaming footprint: "The business is always important but I want consumers to experience our innovation."Beyond digital infrastructure, nation building requires fierce cultural stewardship. This household-led framework views corporate success as a catalyst for preserving national identity. Noting that foreign companies have historically dominated the sector, the documentary asserts, "There was no reason why an Indian company should not be leading the charts on media."Through Jio Studios, the mandate is bold: "What we want to do is claim back the narrative of India, especially young India." By backing massive commercial cinema alongside globally recognised projects, the conglomerate is actively shaping India's cultural footprint. Furthermore, spaces like the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre serve a dual purpose. "The vision of Mrs. Ambani and the vision of our centre is bringing the best of the world to India and the best of India to the world," the film notes.As the company approaches its 50th year, it stands at a critical juncture. Mukesh Ambani frames this generational shift not as a standard corporate handover, but as a continuation of core values. "Akash, Isha and Anant are only representatives of the young leaders," he explains. "And they will take our values. They will build an India of our dreams."At its heart, the enterprise remains anchored by its dining table roots. "To me, family is everything. I feel privileged that four generations of our family live together," shares Nita Ambani. This restless drive is perhaps best captured by 88-year-old V. Balasubramanian, who has spent 62 years at Reliance. He shares, "When I go away from this world, Dhirubhai is waiting there. We will start another Reliance Industries there and start working there and building up another empire. "Ultimately, the Reliance narrative suggests that India's economic rise is deeply intertwined with business models that align commercial scale with societal care. By treating a nation as an extended family, the company offers a compelling, distinctly Indian blueprint for modern nation building.
Article Summary: Reliance documentary, 'Parvah Hai Toh Parivar Hai', pulls back the curtain on this machinery. It offers a case study of what happens when the ethics of a household extend to a conglomerate employing hundreds of thousands, and ultimately to a nation of 1.4 billion people.

Article Title: 'A particular issue': Penguin India on impasse over Sonia Gandhi memoir
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Monday said publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the author’s representatives reached an “impasse over a particular issue. ” The publisher also firmly denied that any external pressure had influenced the decision.Penguin India said the disagreement emerged during its normal editorial review of Belonging: A Journey of Love, which it had been keen to publish.The clarification came amid a growing political controversy over the memoir’s India publication, after Alfred A Knopf, the US-based imprint of Penguin Random House, announced that the book would be released worldwide on November 10. While Congress leaders have raised questions about possible governmental pressure and freedom of expression, Penguin India said the disagreement was strictly part of the editorial process.“On some, they agreed to changes and on others, we accepted the author’s position. Unfortunately, and ultimately, an understanding could not be reached on a particular issue,” the publisher said.PRHI spokesperson Pallavi Narayan said the publishing house had been “really keen” to bring out the memoir, describing it as “a hard-won acquisition”.“We feel it is important for us to correct certain misrepresentations regarding the forthcoming memoir 'Belonging'. This is a book that we at Penguin Random House India, were really keen on publishing as it was a hard-won acquisition,” Narayan said in an exclusive statement to PTI.The publisher said the manuscript had gone through its “normal editorial process”, during which several points were raised and discussed with the author’s representatives. Some proposed changes were accepted, while on other matters Penguin India accepted the author’s position.It was ultimately the unresolved issue that brought the publication process to a halt, according to PRHI. The author’s team subsequently informed the publisher that they did not wish to proceed with the publication, a decision the publishing house said it respected.At the same time, Penguin India rejected suggestions that the impasse was the result of intervention from outside the publishing process.“Since the content of the book is confidential and under embargo, there was no external pressure whatsoever,” the publisher said.PRHI declined to reveal the nature of the disputed issue, citing its contractual obligations and commitment to author confidentiality.“Since we are bound by an agreement, and author confidentiality is paramount to us, we will not divulge details of what led to the impasse,” the publisher said.The publishing house also defended its decision to scrutinise the manuscript, saying editorial assessment, questioning, fact-checking and recommendations were part of its responsibility as a publisher.“As publishers, it was its “responsibility and duty” to critically assess a manuscript, ask questions, make recommendations and exercise its independent editorial judgement,” Penguin India said.The controversy intensified after reports that Penguin India had backed out of publishing the memoir following disagreements over editorial changes. Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot alleged that pressure had been put on Penguin India to remove sections concerning Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the RSS and China’s occupation of Indian territory during the Modi government.Former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Kamal Nath also questioned whether the publisher’s position had been influenced by pressure from elsewhere.Penguin India’s latest statement, however, maintains that no such external intervention took place and that the disagreement arose solely during the editorial process.The memoir is expected to offer a rare account of Gandhi’s life, covering her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family, the assassination of her husband and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, and her subsequent entry into politics.While the international edition is scheduled for release on November 10, the status of its publication in India remains unresolved.
Article Summary: Penguin Random House India said publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the author's representatives reached an “impasse over a particular issue” The publisher also firmly denied that any external pressure had influenced the decision.

Article Title: PM Modi meets Iran president who seeks India's help to end war
Article Text:

PM Narendra Modi called for freedom of navigation and commerce while stressing that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including commercial shipping and seafarers, must not be harmed under any circumstances in a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the margins of the SCO summit in Bishkek. Despite the threat of US sanctions, both leaders backed efforts to expand trade ties.The leaders discussed the West Asia situation, including the Strait of Hormuz situation and Chabahar port cooperation amid the threat of US sanctions, in what was their first formal bilateral meeting in nearly 2 years. Modi expressed concern over escalation of tensions and reiterated the significance of resolving all issues through dialogue and diplomacy, while seeking lasting peace and stability in the region.Blaming the US for failing to fulfil its commitments and declaring that continuation of war is not in the interest of humanity, Pezeshkian urged Modi to use India's "extensive" contacts to wean away parties involved from the path of bloodshed and war. The president also called for expanding bilateral cooperation in political, economic, scientific, cultural and other areas of mutual interest, saying this would neutralise the impact of sanctions and further elevate the relationship.Modi and Pezeshkian last had a bilateral meeting on the margins of the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024. It provided an opportunity for both leaders to reaffirm their commitment to expanding economic cooperation, as Modi underlined India’s commitment to strengthening its long-standing “friendship” with Iran across diverse sectors.“We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come. We had a discussion on the prevailing situation in the region. India will continue to support all efforts aimed at ensuring lasting peace," said Modi in a post on X.According to an Iranian readout, Pezeshkian told Modi that despite efforts by the US and Israel to create roadblocks in Iran's ties with other countries, Tehran was ready to expand its cooperation with India across various fields.The readout also said that Modi backed Pezeshkian's view regarding the existence of groups that see their interests in the continuation of war. “I agree with you that there are those who see their interests in war, but we must intensify our efforts to establish peace. My belief and conviction is that, ultimately, peace and security will prevail," said Modi, according to Iran.Modi also reiterated India's readiness to closely cooperate with Iran in multilateral organizations, including BRICS and SCO and told Pezeshkian he was looking forward to welcoming him for the BRICS Summit in India.“From what I have come to know of your personality, you are a peace-loving person, and I believe that you can play an effective role in advancing the cause of peace. I am confident that your efforts will ultimately lead to positive results,” said Modi in the meeting, according to the Iranian readout.The PM was also quoted as saying that Iran and India have ancient and deep-rooted relations and this historical and cultural heritage can serve as a valuable foundation for expanding cooperation. Transportation and maritime affairs, developments related to the Strait of Hormuz, and progress in Chabahar port cooperation were among the most important issues discussed by the two sides, said the Iranian statement.

The leaders discussed the West Asia situation, including the Strait of Hormuz situation and Chabahar port cooperation. Despite the threat of US sanctions, both leaders backed efforts to expand trade ties.

Article Title: PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
Article Text:
PM Modi during his visit to meet naval personnel aboard INS Vikrant (left); Rahul Gandhi during 'Chhattron ki Goonj' programme (right)

What would it take to dress for Gen Z?

From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style. Their clothes have helped construct identities, signal ideology, project modernity, invoke tradition and increasingly generate the kind of visual moments that social media loves.So when Rahul Gandhi appeared in a pink shirt and later in a yellow one, the change from his usual white clothing drew attention online. The yellow shirt, along with the line "Smash the patriarchy", became part of the social-media conversation. The interest was less about the shirt itself and more about how unusual it looked compared with his regular public appearance.But this is not the first time that a politician's attire has made more headlines than their speech. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's clothes have often drawn attention, from his signature jackets and bandhgalas to the regional outfits he wears during visits across the country. Over the years, they have become a familiar part of his public image.As designer Gaurav Jai Gupta puts it, "Fashion can communicate before a politician has spoken a single word. Clothing conveys identity, ideology, relatability, authority and even regional or cultural affiliation almost instantly." Politics, he adds, is fundamentally about perception, and "an outfit can become the visual shorthand for an entire political moment.Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding.His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. The signature kurta, sleeveless jackets and bandhgalas have become instantly recognisable, while his international appearances often combine Indian craftsmanship with global tailoring.Some of the looks have become headline-makers in their own right.His wardrobe has since offered plenty of other visual moments.A burgundy bandhgala during his first overseas trip as prime minister created a polished diplomatic look. A signature khadi kurta during his Bhutan visit emphasised Indian textiles and craftsmanship. In Nepal, saffron attire paired with a rudraksh mala made a strong cultural and religious statement at Pashupatinath Temple.This habit of dressing for the country he's visiting — or the region of India he's in — is itself a strategy, according to Gupta: "I would definitely consider it a form of fashion diplomacy. Clothing can be a very subtle way of acknowledging the culture of the country you are visiting while siultaneously representing your own identity." Retaining elements of one's own traditional identity alongside that, he says, "reinforces national representation. "His recent looks have been more state-centric. From sporting the gamcha look in Bihar, to a turban in Punjab, and even the traditional mund in Kerala, Modi has worn his "vocals for locals" tag.For years, Rahul Gandhi's public wardrobe has largely stayed within the safe territory of political dressing — white kurta-pajamas, jackets and understated casual wear. It is a familiar uniform in Indian politics, one that keeps the focus on the politician rather than the clothes.But the pink and yellow shirts were different.Bright, instantly noticeable and far removed from the monochrome political wardrobe, they became an unlikely talking point. Gupta explains why a single garment can take on a life entirely of its own online: "The internet loves symbols that are simple, recognisable and easy to reproduce. A yellow shirt is, in itself, just a yellow shirt. But once social media attaches a narrative to it, the garment can acquire an entirely new meaning. " The audience, he says, effectively co-authors the outfit's significance — "memes, edits, captions and commentary can transform an ordinary look into a cultural reference point," helped along by the fact that "colour is highly emotional and visually immediate."He did not wear it just anywhere, either. He wore it to the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' programme, where the audience was predominantly Gen Z. But this is not the first time the Leader of Opposition has made news for his fashion. In 2019, Rahul attended a Kerala college event in a t-shirt and jeans, taking a break from his classic white kurta look, with his "You can call me Rahul" reels still going viral.Likewise, it was not a conincidence that he went with a blue t-shirt, when he held up the red book in his hand and said "Save the Constitution", or a black one to protest outside the Parliament.It's a pattern. Every Rahul Gandhi's politics has reflected in his preference for colours.If PM Modi's wardrobe demonstrates the power of personal branding, the Thackerays show how colour and clothing can become political shorthand.Bal Thackeray initially adopted the shirt-and-trouser look of the urban office worker, appealing to an aspirational Maharashtra audience. Later, as Hindutva became central to his political positioning, orange became a defining element of his public appearance.Fashion designer Nivedita Saboo, who has dressed several politicians, explains why colour carries this kind of political weight in the first place: "Colour communicates emotion before language does. Saffron can evoke spirituality, sacrifice, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity. White can communicate simplicity, peace, authority or the traditional Gandhian vocabulary. Electric or deep blue has powerful associations with social justice, equality and Ambedkarite politics. " But, she cautions, "colour is never universal. Its meaning changes with culture, history, political association, fabric, styling and even the person's body language. That's why political dressing is fascinating: you can say something without saying anything."Uddhav Thackeray developed his own visual identity through simple, brightly coloured sadra-pajamas closely associated with Maharashtrian culture.Aaditya Thackeray, meanwhile, represents another generational shift, combining traditional Indian clothing with contemporary fashion.Three generations. Three styles. And three different ways of speaking to their audiences without saying a word.Then there are politicians whose biggest fashion statement is that they appear to have made very little effort at all.Mamata Banerjee's white cotton saree with a blue border and hawai chappals have become almost inseparable from her political identity. Arvind Kejriwal's muffler achieved a similar status.The appeal is simple: don't look like a politician; look like the people who vote for you. As Gupta puts it, "politics is about recognition and relatability, not necessarily luxury." A consistent, uncomplicated look, he says, "can become incredibly powerful because people can immediately identify it" — Mamata Banerjee's saree and Kejriwal's muffler "function almost like logos," communicating accessibility in a way an expensive designer wardrobe rarely can. "In a country like ours, simplicity is more relatable," he says. "In mass politics, that emotional connection can be far more valuable than sartorial sophistication."The repetition is what makes it powerful. Eventually, the garment becomes a logo.See the white-and-blue saree, think Mamata. See the muffler, think Kejriwal. See the kurta and jacket, think Modi.And now, in the age of viral fashion moments, perhaps even a yellow shirt can enter the political visual dictionary.When Vijay took oath as Tamil Nadu chief minister, he broke from the traditional white shirt-and-veshti look, arriving instead in a sharply tailored black suit. He has since made black-and-white suits a regular part of his public image.Addressing the attention around his wardrobe, Vijay said, “Many people have been talking about the new suit that I have been wearing recently. Are we not allowed to wear a coat and suit? Is it meant only for people in positions of authority? There is nothing like that.”Explaining his choice, he added, “I am not wearing many colours. It is just black and white, like all our hearts. The choice of these colours is to show that I will remain transparent and simple in everything, just like black and white.”Long before politicians had to worry about going viral, Indira Gandhi had already mastered the art of having a recognisable political look.Her sarees, from Banarasi silk to handlooms and Tanchois, became an important part of her public image. They projected tradition and authority at the same time, allowing her to appear deeply rooted in Indian culture while commanding political spaces at home and abroad.The saree wasn't simply a sartorial choice. The way she wore it, with the pallu covering her head from the loose end of the saree, made it distinct.Gupta points to exactly this kind of repetition as the foundation of a political fashion identity: "Consistency is the key to creating a fashion identity. When a politician repeatedly wears a particular silhouette, colour palette, accessory or garment, it becomes part of their visual vocabulary." Indira Gandhi's sarees, he notes, "became inseparable from her public image," much "like branding in fashion or advertising: repetition creates recognition. " Eventually, he says, "you don't need to see the entire person; a particular silhouette, colour combination or accessory can be enough to trigger recognition." But he's careful to add a caveat: "successful political style usually feels authentic rather than overly constructed. The strongest personal brands emerge when the clothes reinforce something the politician already represents."For women in politics especially, clothing has always carried an extra layer of scrutiny. Too traditional, and a leader can be boxed into convention. Too Western, and questions about cultural authenticity can follow.Moreover, most female political leaders of the time or the ones who preceeded her wore sarees the same way.Indira's style largely sidestepped that binary. She made traditional Indian clothing look powerful.The political fashion story goes back even further.Jawaharlal Nehru's iconic jacket became so closely associated with him that his name effectively became part of the garment's identity. The jacket was a descendant of the northern Indian achkan, a closed-neck, coat-like garment traditionally associated with Indian nobility. It was largely when the style was marketed to Western audiences that it took the "Nehru" name, after the prime minister popularised it through his public appearances. The minimalist look later found fans beyond politics, including the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr, who reportedly owned more than 200 Nehru jackets.Khadi and handlooms carried an even bigger political history, associated with nationalism, self-reliance and the freedom movement.Then came Rajiv Gandhi.Dark sunglasses, sneakers, sleeveless fleece jackets and khadi kurta-pajamas gave him a distinctly more contemporary appearance. His wardrobe reflected the image he projected politically — younger, modern and more comfortable with the technological future.In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.Fidel Castro, meanwhile, swapped the traditional military and political imagery for tracksuits later in life. He was famously photographed wearing a red, white and blue Adidas tracksuit while recovering from surgery in 2006. The look soon became part of his public image, with Castro later wearing sportswear from brands including Fila, Puma and Nike.If a yellow shirt at a college event can trend for days, the question naturally follows: what does it actually take for a politician's wardrobe to land with a generation raised on Instagram and short-form video?Saboo, who has worked closely with politicians on exactly this brief, is blunt about the trap most of them fall into. "Gen Z has grown up in a visual culture where identity is communicated through what you wear," she says. "But breaking the dress code simply to look young can backfire. Gen Z is extremely good at detecting what feels manufactured. The clothes have to feel like the person, not like a stylist has dressed them to look young. " A politician who "wears the traditional kurta beautifully and owns it completely," she argues, can be "far more compelling than somebody wearing sneakers and a T-shirt because someone told them that's what young people like." For her, the real shift isn't from tradition to trend — it's "from dress code to personal code."Asked to imagine one outfit that could say "young India" without a single slogan, she describes something quietly hybrid: a relaxed, engineered jacket in a lightweight Indian textile over a tapered trouser, perhaps a modernised kurta with sharper, almost architectural proportions underneath, finished with one unexpected element — an unusual seam, a technical fabric panel, a monogram, a contemporary sneaker.The palette, she says, would be "sophisticated rather than loud — ivory, charcoal, deep blue or earthy neutrals with one energetic accent." The test, in her words: "It shouldn't look like 'politician trying to be fake and dress young.' It should look like India's next generation has naturally evolved its own version of Indian clothing."Her advice to politicians boils down to five principles: don't dress younger, dress more authentically; modernise proportions rather than identity; find one recurring signature — a colour, a silhouette, a jacket, a watch — rather than constantly changing the wardrobe; make sure the clothes actually function in a country that "lives fast"; and, above all, stop being afraid of personality. As she puts it, "politics has traditionally rewarded conformity. Gen Z is attracted to people who appear comfortable in their own skin." Fashion, she concludes, "cannot manufacture relatability. It can only amplify it."
Article Summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding. His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style.

Article Title: First exam reforms, now 'school thik karo' campaign: How CJP is changing the discourse of politics
Article Text:
School students protest in UP

CJP claims credit

Political parties take a cue from CJP

Youth outreach

NEW DELHI: From colleges to schools. From Gen Z to Gen Alpha. From Jantar Mantar to cities and villages in states. The students’ protest has continued; only the stage has shifted. The Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “School Thik Karo” campaign has put the spotlight on the sorry condition of government schools in many states. Gen Z showed the way from Jantar Mantar when they forced the NDA government to make Dharmendra Pradhan resign over NEET paper leaks. Gen Alpha took the cue and brought the protests to villages and towns across states, demanding better school infrastructure and government accountability.The CJP campaign asking for school audits in villages got a huge response. The pictures and videos of schools uploaded on CJP’s X timeline exposed the sorry state of government schools across states. This was followed by ground inspections by CJP teams, which led to confrontation and a strong pushback by some state governments.Two days after the CJP launched its campaign and announced that schools in Rajasthan would be on its radar, the state education department issued new guidelines regulating the entry of outsiders, including media personnel, into government schools.Under the directives, photography, videography, interviews, audio recording and live streaming involving students or school activities on campus needed prior permission from the school principal or head of the institution.The Rajasthan order went on to threaten action under applicable laws in case of any breach.So, when a CJP team went to inspect a government school on August 21, it was attacked and forcibly pushed back, allegedly by the locals. Videos of the incident showed a large number of people engaging in a heated exchange with the CJP team, pushing and shoving its members as they tried to enter the village. Some clips also showed stone-pelting and smashed windows of cars. Locals said the village did not need outside political groups to intervene in the school’s affairs.This perhaps became the July 20 Jantar Mantar moment (when Delhi Police used force to stop Gen Z protesters from their Sansad march) of the CJP school campaign as the violent confrontation propelled the issue to the national centre stage.Meanwhile in Uttar Pradesh, Gen Alpha students of a government school staged a protest twice, in a span of four days. over shortage of subject teachers. They briefly blocked traffic also. Students of a government school in Kannauj boycotted classes and held protests against the principal for alleged caste discrimination and ordering the felling of trees inside the school campus. The students of PM Shri Composite School in Gugarapur surrounded the vehicle of the in-charge principal at the school gate as he was leaving and raised slogans against him.Protests also happened in Fatehpur, Hamirpur against lack of facilities in schools. In Hamirpur, 'Gen Alpha' children laid siege to the collectorate to demand the construction of a paved road to their school.In Unnao, hundreds of students of a government-run residential school staged a protest over alleged poor-quality food, inadequate drinking water, shortage of teachers and the behaviour of the principal, briefly disrupting traffic at a city crossing.In Maharashtra, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke conducted a social audit of government-run and municipal schools in Latur district. He led a team at a Zilla Parishad school at Ujani village in Latur's Ausa tehsil.After his audit, Dipke said schools in the state were in a pitiable condition, and even "ministers’ dogs got better facilities" than students. He sought the resignation of Maharashtra school education minister Dada Bhuse. Later, Maharashtra police registered a case against the CJP convenor and others for allegedly entering a government school without permission, disrupting official work and threatening teachers.The state governments cited rules to browbeat the CJP teams away from its schools. But at the same time, they were forced to act to nullify the impact of the CJP campaign. So, while some states announced new measures to improve the condition of schools, others increased the pace of work already underway to ensure that results were seen on the ground quickly.The CJP was quick to claim credit for govt actions and basked in glory.“The impact we’ve been able to make with such a small team in such a short span of time is just unreal. Multiple state governments have had to bow down. Authorities had to listen to Gen Z and Gen Alpha kids and give them their due,” it said in a post on X.“But this does not end here. We need to keep going until even the remotest regions of the nation, even the most deprived communities, have access to the highest standard of educational facilities. They may use force, they may file cases, they may do whatever they can to crush this, but we will remain committed to the same demand,” the post read.While it can be debated whether or not the CJP campaign forced the governments into action, what can be said with certainty is that the CJP has managed to do what many political parties could not - inspire the youth to come to the streets and seek accountability from power.The two CJP campaigns also point to an interesting shift - which should be a learning lesson, especially for parties in the opposition space. We have seen the opposition parties raise the pitch against government on issues like caste and religion as these have greater potential for voter mobilisation. Rarely do we see campaigns by the opposition parties centred around health or education reforms. But that seems to have changed.The Congress has taken a cue and is trying to stay focused on students’ connect and raise issues that concern the youth. In Rajasthan, the state Congress unit is also on the streets to highlight gaps in state government school infrastructure.And it’s not just the opposition that is course-correcting; the ruling BJP has also drawn a roadmap to engage with the youth and understand their concerns. In the middle of the Gen Z protest, Prime Minister Narendra Modi debuted on Instagram and tried to communicate directly with the youth who were on the streets. The BJP has in fact formed a dedicated team to spearhead its Gen Z outreach. The team includes BJP chief Nitin Nabin, national general secretaries Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde, Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi, Chhattisgarh minister OP Choudhary, along with several other leaders.Clearly, the CJP has managed to change the political discourse and has put the focus on the youth as potential game-changers in electoral politics. As we gear up for the next rounds of assembly elections in the run-up to the 2029 Lok Sabha challenge, we may see youth outreach taking centre stage like never before.
Article Summary: The Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “School Thik Karo’ campaign has put the spotlight on the sorry condition of government schools in many states. Gen Z showed the way from Jantar Mantar when they forced the NDA government to make Dharmendra Pradhan resign over NEET paper leaks.

NEW DELHI: The five-member Supreme Court Collegium led by CJI Surya Kant on Monday recommended the appointment of Justice Sanjay K Agrawal as chief justice of Rajasthan, whose acting chief justice S P Sharma has recused himself from judicial work following allegations regarding his integrity levelled by SC judge Sandeep Mehta.In a fast-paced development, the controversy sparked by Justice Mehta’s three letters within two weeks to CJI Kant seeking appointment of a regular CJ to Rajasthan HC gained momentum with advocates at the HC indulging in sloganeering against the acting CJ, followed by Justice Sharma recusing from judicial work and culminating late evening on Monday by the Collegium recommending Justice Agarwal of Chhattisgarh HC as the CJ of Rajasthan HC.The Collegium, also comprising Justices Vikram Nath, B V Nagarathna, M M Sundresh and P S Narasimha, recommended appointment of Justice Alpesh Yeshwant Kogje of Gujarat HC as CJ of Madhya Pradesh HC and Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati of Rajasthan HC as the CJ of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh HC.As the present CJ of Chhattisgarh HC, Justice Ramesh Sinha, is retiring on Sep 4, the Collegium recommended the appointment of Justice Krushna Ram Mohapatra as the CJ of Chhattisgarh consequent to the retirement of Justice Sinha.Curiously, the first resolution of the Collegium recommended only the transfer of Justice Sanjay Agrawal to Rajasthan HC without specifying his appointment as its CJ, which was specified in the subsequent resolution uploaded on the SC website shortly thereafter. Justice Sharma, who has been at the eye of a storm created by letters from Justice Mehta to the CJI, is scheduled to retire on Sep 26.
Article Summary: The five-member Supreme Court Collegium led by CJI Surya Kant on Monday recommended the appointment of Justice Sanjay K Agrawal as chief justice of Rajasthan. Acting chief justice S P Sharma has recused himself from judicial work following allegations regarding his integrity levelled by Sandeep Mehta.

Article Title: IMD predicts below-normal rainfall over country in September
Article Text:
India to witness above avg temperature in September; rainfall likely to be below normal

NEW DELHI: Monthly rainfall over the country as a whole is most likely to be below normal in Sept, the last month of the monsoon season, said IMD Monday - an indication that the four-month rainy season is likely to end with overall deficient cumulative rainfall, as was predicted earlier due to the impact of El Nino.IMD said Aug, which reported a deficit of more than 16% in monthly rainfall in the country despite good rains in certain parts, was the warmest Aug in India since 1901, recording a mean temperature of 28.010°C.Region-wise, South peninsular India recorded its second-warmest Aug since 1901. East and northeast India recorded their third-warmest, while northwest India saw its fifth-warmest, Aug in 126 years.So far, the country as a whole has reported a deficit of 14% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 31) rainfall, despite ‘normal’ rainfall in July. In June, the deficit was as high as 35%. Out of a total of 741 districts assessed for monsoon rainfall distribution, 312 (42%) received ‘below-normal’ rainfall and 38 districts (5%) reported large deficient rainfall till Aug 31.A forecast of ‘below-normal’ rainfall in Sept may lead to a deficit in overall kharif acreage. Though the sowing of most seasonal crops is almost complete, with a decline in acreage of nearly 2% compared with the corresponding period last year, low rainfall in Sept implies an increase in input cost due to farmers’ spending on irrigation of standing crops.“Spatially, many parts of the country are likely to receive below-normal rainfall, but some areas of northwest, northeast, east, east-central and south-east peninsular India are likely to receive ‘normal to above-normal’ rainfall,” said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.He said “strong El Niño conditions” are currently prevailing over the equatorial Pacific Ocean, with sea surface temperature remaining above normal across central and eastern equatorial Pacific. “These conditions are expected to strengthen further in the coming months,” said Mohapatra, hinting at its negative impact on Sept rainfall.El Niño is invariably associated with a weak monsoon and a harsh summer in India.At present, neutral Indian Ocean Dipole conditions prevail over Indian Ocean, which are likely to persist through Sept.This means that monsoon may not benefit from this climatic phenomenon as only positive IOD helps increase rainfall activities.
Article Summary: IMD said Aug, which reported a deficit of more than 16% in monthly rainfall in the country despite good rains in certain parts, was the warmest Aug in India since 1901. In June, the deficit was as high as 35%. Out of a total of 741 districts assessed for monsoon rainfall distribution, 312 received ‘below- normal’ rainfall.

Article Title: Not the era of war to end of war: PM Modi reiterates peace message to Putin
Article Text:

With still no end in sight to the Russia-Ukraine war, PM Narendra Modi renewed his message of peace to Russian President Vladimir Putin saying on this occasion that it was time to move from an endless war to the end of war for the sake of humanity.Modi delivered the message in his opening remarks before a bilateral meeting with Putin on the margins of the SCO heads of state summit in Bishkek in which the leaders focused on expanding cooperation in energy, defence, innovation, space, fertilisers and people-to-people linkages.The endless war to end of war message is the latest in a series of televised statements by Modi before Putin for the return of peace, beginning with his assertion in 2022 - frequently cited by the Western world and even making it to the G20 Bali Declaration that year - that this wasn't the era of war. That message too was delivered on the margins of another SCO summit in Samarkand. He followed it up with a message to Putin in Moscow in 2024 - in the midst of an outrage in the West over his Russia visit - that no solution can be found on the battlefield.Modi told Putin in Bishkek that India supports all efforts for peace and will continue to do so in the future, adding that an early end to the war was the call of humanity and also the message from the land of Buddha and Gandhi.“Every day spent in the war pushes humanity back. And every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We will have to move from an endless war to an end of war, which is very important for humanity's well-being,” said the PM.“That all issues are resolved peacefully as soon as possible is the call of humanity. This is the message of India. This is the message of the land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha - the path to peace,” said Modi, adding that he was looking forward to welcoming Putin for the BRICS summit. India's balancing act on the war saw Modi travelling to Ukraine a few months after his visit to Russia in 2024.According to foreign secretary Vikram Misri, Modi conveyed to Putin India's readiness to do whatever is feasible and necessary at India's end to move the conflict towards an end because "it is exacting a very heavy toll on the global community at large"."Had extensive discussions with President Putin. Discussed the full range of the India-Russia Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership. It is gladdening to see significant progress across various sectors in recent years," said Modi in a post on X.In his own televised statement, Putin acknowledged Modi's personal attention to the development of bilateral ties. Putin also said Russia was preparing "seriously" for the BRICS summit in India and highlighted that over the past 10 years, the number of Indian students in Russia has shot up to 40,000.According to an Indian readout, the leaders exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral arena, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026. “They also shared perspectives on key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers,” said the Indian readout, adding that Modi reiterated dialogue and diplomacy was the way forward in resolving conflicts.The two leaders agreed to remain in touch to further strengthen the partnership, acknowledging its growth and resilience against the backdrop of geopolitical uncertainties.
Article Summary: Modi delivered the message in his opening remarks before a bilateral meeting with Putin on the margins of the SCO heads of state summit in Bishkek. The leaders focused on expanding cooperation in energy, defence, innovation, space, fertilisers and people-to-people linkages. Putin acknowledged Modi's personal attention to the development of bilateral ties.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to pass any interim orders on two PILs, including one by a retired police officer, seeking deferment of Cockroach Janata Party ‘s proposed march on Sep 5 by alleging that it is intended to create lawlessness ahead of Sep 12-13 BRICS summit in Delhi to deter participation of world leaders.When the petitioners questioned how such a march from the India Gate to the Police Headquarters can take place without permission, A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there are two issues – one relates to law and order and the other to policy relating to permission to protest marches.“Let the stakeholders talk to them. As of now we have no reason to doubt that everyone would act and behave in a very responsible manner and in a peaceful and lawful manner. Right now, there is no compelling reason for us (the court) to presume that any wrong will happen. It is for the law enforcing agencies to ensure law and order while acting in accordance with law,” the CJI-led bench said.Appearing for one of the petitioners, advocate Syed Rizwan Ahmed said given the BRICS summit, till date no application seeking permission has been given to the authorities. In West Bengal, the previous govt did not give permission to so many protest rallies and the organizers had to move the HC for permission.Why does CJP, an unregistered entity not follow the same process? Are they above law, he asked.“God forbid another mishap, may not be by CJP, but by some mischievous elements take place, it will be covered by international media and deter participation of the foreign country leaders in BRICs,” he apprehended.The bench said, “All these factors are to be considered by some other quarters, not by us. There is nothing we can say right now. If something untoward or alarming happens, then file an application before us, provided the issue falls for determination in judicial domain.”The bench issued notice to the Centre on the two PILs, asked them to supply copies to the SC-constituted High-Powered Committee headed by retired SC judge R Subhash Reddy as well as the office of the solicitor general and posted these for hearing on Sep 10 along with petitions on July 20 incidents during protest march to Parliament, which turned violent resulting in alleged police excesses, injuries to protesters and security personnel and damage to public and private properties.When Ahmed asked whether CJP is above law and its processes, the bench said, “These are issues which are to be taken care of by the law and order enforcing agencies. Article Title: SC: Externment orders cannot be passed routinely, require reasons
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Holding that forcing a person to stay out of a city or district affects freedom guaranteed by the Constitution, SC on Monday ruled that a govt cannot pass an externment order routinely and must pass a reasoned order to justify such harsh measures.A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed an externment order passed by Raigarh district magistrate directing a person to remove himself from the district and contiguous districts for one year. The order was passed against him as multiple criminal cases were pending and the district authority apprehended that his presence would create further problems in the area and nearby districts.“An order of externment directly impinges upon valuable fundamental freedoms guaranteed to a citizen and, therefore, cannot be made as a matter of routine. Further, merely because multiple criminal cases have been filed against a person would not, ipso facto, be a ground for ordering externment,” the bench said.Before exercising such power, the DM is required to arrive at a bona fide and informed subjective satisfaction that circumstances warrant such an extreme measure and externment is necessary, it said.The bench said the authority is not expected to render a judgement as a court of law but the order must nonetheless disclose, at least in broad terms, the reasons for such satisfaction.“The existence of objective material and a discernible nexus between such material and the conclusion reached are indispensable safeguards against arbitrary exercise of power,” it said.Quashing the order under Chhattisgarh Rajya Suraksha Adhiniyam, SC said the externment order fell short of statutory requirement. “The order does not indicate the material on the basis of which such conclusion was reached. No reasons are forthcoming to demonstrate why the third respondent (Raipur DM) considered the situation grave enough to necessitate the appellant’s externment,” it said.
Article Summary: SC quashes Raigarh DM order, says multiple criminal cases alone not grounds for such action. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed an externment order. The order was passed against him as multiple criminal Cases were pending and the district authority apprehended that his presence would create further problems.
